title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
summary: Specifies DHCPv6, which lets servers hand out configuration such as IPv6 addresses and other parameters to IPv6 hosts. It can allocate reusable addresses automatically and offers extra configuration flexibility. It is the stateful counterpart to stateless address autoconfiguration and can be used with it. It was replaced by RFC 8415.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a new network, you need an address and some settings. DHCPv6 is like a front desk that hands you your room number and a welcome sheet.

questions: how do ipv6 hosts get addresses from a server
what is a duid in dhcpv6
subtitle: The original DHCP for IPv6: servers hand out addresses and settings, with relays, leases and identifiers.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts need a managed way to receive addresses and other configuration such as DNS and NTP servers, and a way for administrators to control who gets what.
tldr.mechanism: A client discovers servers by multicast over UDP, using a four-message Solicit, Advertise, Request, Reply exchange or a two-message shortcut. Each address carries lifetimes that the client extends with Renew and Rebind. Relay agents carry messages across links.
tldr.outcome: This is the stateful counterpart to stateless address autoconfiguration. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8415 and updated by many later RFCs.

today: RFC 3315 has been obsoleted by RFC 8415, which is the current DHCPv6 specification. It has also been updated by RFC 4361, RFC 5494, RFC 6221, RFC 6422, RFC 6644, RFC 7083, RFC 7227, RFC 7283 and RFC 7550.

sections.title: What DHCPv6 Does
sections.content:
RFC 3315 describes DHCP for IPv6, a client/server protocol that provides managed configuration of devices. A DHCP server can give a device addresses and other configuration, carried in options, and new options can be defined later. The RFC calls DHCP the stateful address autoconfiguration protocol referred to in RFC 2462, and compatibility with stateless address autoconfiguration is a design requirement.

DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 work differently enough that the RFC leaves any integration between them out.

Clients and servers exchange messages over UDP. A client uses its link-local address and sends most messages to a reserved link-scoped multicast address, so it does not need to know any server address in advance. A relay agent on the client's link can carry messages to servers on other links, transparently to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device does not know who is in charge, so it shouts a question to everyone nearby. Whoever runs the network answers with the settings it should use.

sections.title: Message Exchanges
sections.content:
A client that only needs settings, such as DNS or NTP server lists, sends an Information-Request to the multicast address FF02::1:2 and gets a Reply. No addresses are assigned.

To get addresses, the client usually uses four messages. It sends Solicit to find servers, any suitable server answers with Advertise, the client picks one and sends Request, and the server confirms with Reply. If the client includes a Rapid Commit option in its Solicit and a server is willing to commit, two messages are enough: Solicit then Reply.

Each address has a preferred lifetime and a valid lifetime. The client sends Renew to the server that gave the address to extend them, and Rebind to any server if Renew gets no answer. Other messages are Confirm (check the addresses still fit the link), Release (give addresses back) and Decline (an address is already in use on the link).

Servers can also start an exchange. A Reconfigure message tells a client to start a Renew or Information-request exchange, for example when links are being renumbered. Because of the risk of denial of service, the server MUST use DHCP authentication in Reconfigure.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks who can help, helpers answer, it picks one, and that one confirms. Later it checks back in to keep its address, like renewing a library book.

sections.title: Message Formats and Constants
sections.content:
Client and server messages share one fixed header: a 1-octet msg-type and a 3-octet transaction-id, followed by options. All values are in network byte order, and options are packed with no padding. Clients listen on UDP port 546, and servers and relay agents on UDP port 547.

Thirteen message types are defined, numbered 1 to 13 from SOLICIT (1) through RELAY-REPL (13), with REPLY as 7 and RECONFIGURE as 10.

Relay messages use a different header: msg-type, hop-count, a link-address that tells the server which link the client is on, and a peer-address. A Relay-forward message wraps the received message inside a Relay Message option, and the server answers with a Relay-reply that copies the hop-count, link-address and peer-address. A relay may relay through other relays, and the limit HOP_COUNT_LIMIT is 32.

Options are the extension mechanism. For example, the IA_NA option (option code 3) carries an identity association identifier, the times T1 and T2, and the addresses. The Rapid Commit option is code 14 with length 0. The value 0xffffffff means infinity for lifetimes, T1 and T2.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message begins with a short note saying what kind it is and a ticket number. Everything else goes into labeled slots after that, so new slots can be added later.

sections.title: DUIDs and Identity Associations
sections.content:
Every client and server has one DUID (DHCP Unique Identifier). It is a 2-octet type code followed by at most 128 octets of identifier. Peers MUST treat it as an opaque value and compare it only for equality. It should stay stable even if network hardware changes. Three types are defined: link-layer address plus time (type 1), vendor-assigned ID based on an enterprise number (type 2) and link-layer address (type 3). Type 1 MUST NOT be used by devices without stable storage.

An identity association (IA) groups a set of related addresses on one client interface. Each IA has a client-chosen IAID that MUST stay consistent across client restarts, and a type: IA_NA for non-temporary addresses or IA_TA for temporary addresses. The server keeps a binding indexed by the DUID, the IA type and the IAID.

The server picks addresses according to its administrator's policy and what it learns about the client, including the link the client is on.
sections.plainLanguage: A DUID is a name tag that stays the same even if you change your shoes. An identity association is a labeled folder that holds the addresses you were given.

sections.title: Reliability and Retransmission
sections.content:
DHCP runs over UDP, so clients are responsible for reliability. If no response arrives, the client retransmits with a timeout that is randomized by a factor between -0.1 and +0.1 to avoid synchronized clients. The RFC lists default parameters such as SOL_TIMEOUT of 1 sec, SOL_MAX_RT of 120 secs, REQ_MAX_RC of 10, REN_TIMEOUT of 10 secs and REB_MAX_RT of 600 secs.

The first Solicit MUST be delayed by a random time between 0 and SOL_MAX_DELAY (1 sec), which desynchronizes clients that start together, for example after a power outage. The client collects Advertise messages for the first timeout and then SHOULD send a Request. A server preference value of 255 in an Advertise lets the client proceed immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody answers, the device asks again, adding a random pause so a whole street of devices does not shout at once.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
The RFC treats the threat to DHCP as inherently an insider threat. Named attacks include a malicious server giving a client wrong configuration (for example to mount a man-in-the-middle attack on DNS or NTP), a client masquerading as another, and resource exhaustion. A malicious server can send a Reconfigure followed by a Reply, so a client MUST discard any Reconfigure that is not authenticated.

Two authentication mechanisms are defined: the Delayed Authentication protocol, which uses a shared secret key and a DHCP realm, and the Reconfigure Key protocol. DHCP authentication provides authentication and integrity but no privacy for message contents. Communication between relay agents and servers can be secured with IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake front desk could hand out wrong room numbers. So the real desk can prove who it is, especially when it tells you to come back and re-register.
